title: Build Dynamic Products, and Stop the AI Sideshow — Eliza Cabrera (Workday) + Jeremy Silva (Freeplay)

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on AI product design strategy, customer-first development, and the crawl-walk-run framework for building integrated AI products with human-in-the-loop considerations. The framework is cross-domain but illustrated through enterprise HR service delivery and customer support scenarios from Workday and a hypothetical SaaS example. Crawl-walk-run spans early planning through prototyping to production autonomous agents at scale. Familiarity with AI product concepts is assumed but no deep technical model knowledge is required. Recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. Multiple direct transcript excerpts substantiate the product design and human factors classification.

summary: Eliza Cabrera (Principal AI PM at Workday) and Jeremy Silva (Product Lead at Freeplay) present a framework for building 'dynamic products' and avoiding the 'AI sideshow'—the tendency to let AI technology lead product, GTM, and strategy. They trace the evolution from chat UIs and multimodal experiments, through RAG and vector databases for accuracy, co-pilots reflecting discomfort with automation, to agents that reason and use tools. While not wrong, these approaches are undifferentiated because everyone pursues them. Through Freeplay's work across dozens of enterprise companies, they identified why bolt-on AI persists: centralized AI strategies run as sidecars to core product strategy; companies quarantine AI to mitigate reliability risk; teams become hammers seeking nails; and solutions are pushed top-down rather than discovered bottoms-up. The remedy is integrating AI risk into planning with new evaluation and testing muscles, starting with genuine customer problems, and enabling bottoms-up discovery while setting top-level strategy. The north star is AI products deeply and dynamically integrated into the product ecosystem—products that need not announce themselves as AI but simply solve customer problems better. They propose a crawl-walk-run approach: crawl adds embedded AI to existing functionality (e.g., semantic search); walk builds contextual, personalized experiences requiring new surface area but not fundamental architecture changes (e.g., draft suggestions); run creates dynamic, interoperable, integrated AI requiring rethought UI/UX and architecture (e.g., autonomous agents). Eliza illustrates all three phases with Workday's HR service delivery products. Crawl: the Help product where content authors upload long policy documents and AI generates employee FAQs, manager talking points, and translations into 34 languages with version management—built for users unfamiliar with Gen AI, went GA August 2024. Walk: a contextually aware Workday assistant co-pilot spanning the platform (HCM, financials, benefits, procurement), with attention to PII sensitivity in data processing and requiring top-down/bottoms-up alignment across the suite. Run: agentic capabilities behind the Workday assistant tied to an agent system of record, making the assistant more autonomous and proactive—listening to policy changes and notifying users—threaded across product experiences serving 60% of the S&P 500. They close by emphasizing that agents and AI capabilities are stepping stones for training the organization, not ends in themselves. The real destination is dynamic products that extend problem spaces through frictionless multimodal experiences and interoperability.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the AI Sideshow Concept
sections.summary: Eliza and Jeremy introduce themselves and frame the core message: stop the AI sideshow. AI leading product, GTM, and strategy was effective in 2023 but is now undifferentiated. They trace the evolution from chat UIs through RAG, co-pilots, to agents, noting these are technology exploration approaches, not differentiated strategy.

sections.title: Causes of the AI Sideshow
sections.summary: Through Freeplay's enterprise work, they identify causes: centralized AI strategies running as sidecars, risk quarantining AI to product corners, prioritizing technology over customer needs (hammer seeking nail), and top-down solution pushing. Examples include building chatbots and document summarization to demonstrate capability rather than solve real problems.

sections.title: Avoiding the AI Sideshow
sections.summary: The remedy: integrate AI risk into planning with new evaluation and testing muscles, start with the customer problem, and enable bottoms-up discovery while setting top-level strategy. The north star is deeply, dynamically integrated AI products that solve customer problems better without announcing themselves as AI.

sections.title: Crawl-Walk-Run Framework
sections.summary: They introduce the crawl-walk-run approach using a customer support SaaS example. Crawl embeds AI into existing functionality (semantic search for similar questions). Walk builds contextual personalized experiences (draft suggestions). Run creates dynamic interoperable agents requiring rethought UI/UX and architecture. Functionality compounds across phases.

sections.title: Workday Crawl: Help Product and Translations
sections.summary: Eliza presents Workday's Help product for HR service delivery. In the crawl phase, content authors upload long policy documents (e.g., 20+ page benefits policy) and AI generates employee FAQs and manager talking points for content teams of 3-15 people. She adds a translations feature supporting 34 languages with version management for base articles and translations. The design avoided in-your-face sparkles and chatbots, built for users unfamiliar with Gen AI in 2023, keeping the human in the loop with subtle AI indicators. This went GA in August 2024.

sections.title: Workday Walk: Contextually Aware Assistant
sections.summary: Eliza describes the walk phase: a contextually aware Workday assistant co-pilot that lives across the platform, helping users with tasks like location changes. It provides contextually aware suggestions based on the current page and handles data sensitivity appropriately—distinguishing help article content from PII-heavy compensation tasks. As a platform capability spanning HCM, financials, benefits, procurement, and core HCM, this required higher top-down and bottoms-up alignment to ship.

sections.title: Workday Run: Agent System of Record and Dynamic Products
sections.summary: Eliza covers the run phase: Workday's announced agent system of record, with agentic capabilities behind the Workday assistant making it more autonomous and proactive—listening to policy changes and notifying users with suggestions. This threads top-down strategy with bottoms-up execution across product experiences serving 60% of the S&P 500. She closes by emphasizing that agents and AI are stepping stones for training the organization, not final destinations. The real goal is dynamic products that extend problem spaces through frictionless multimodal experiences and interoperability, referencing talks by Sarah and Brian on purposeful vertical-specific products.

demonstrations: Workday Help product crawl: content authors upload a 20+ page benefits policy document and AI ingests it to create employee FAQs and manager talking points in a consistent format
Workday Help translations: in a few clicks, translate generated content into 34 supported languages with version management for base articles and translations

Hypothetical customer support SaaS crawl-walk-run: semantic search surfacing similar past questions (crawl), suggesting draft responses ahead of time (walk), autonomous agent triaging and responding across the product (run)
